title: The Poisoned Arrow
text:
A monk named Malunkyaputta was troubled because the Buddha had never answered certain great questions. Was the world eternal or not? Was it finite or infinite? Were the soul and the body the same thing or different? Did an enlightened one exist after death or not? He went to the Buddha and declared that unless these questions were answered, he would give up his training and return to ordinary life.

The Buddha replied with a story. Suppose a man were struck by an arrow smeared thickly with poison. His friends and family bring a surgeon to treat him. But the wounded man says: I will not let this arrow be pulled out until I know who shot me, whether he was a noble or a priest or a merchant or a worker, what his name and clan are, whether he was tall or short or of medium height, what his skin was like, where he lived. And I want to know what kind of bow he used, what the string was made of, what feathers were on the shaft, and what kind of arrowhead it was.

That man, the Buddha said, would die before he learned any of it. In the same way, he had left those questions unanswered because they did not lead to the end of suffering. What he taught was suffering, its cause, its end and the path to its end.
lesson: When you are in trouble, deal with the wound before the theory. Sort questions by whether answering them changes what you must do now.
location: Jeta's Grove, Savatthi (modern Uttar Pradesh, India)
